topics.name: Nuclear Composition and Size: Isotopes, Isobars, Isotones, and Nuclear Density
topics.summary: A nucleus of element X is written \( {}_Z^A\mathrm{X} \), where the atomic number \( Z \) counts protons and the mass number \( A \) counts all nucleons, so the neutron number is \( A-Z \). Nuclides are grouped by which count they share. Isotopes have the same \( Z \) but different \( A \): the same element with different neutron numbers, such as \( {}_1^1\mathrm{H} \), \( {}_1^2\mathrm{H} \) and \( {}_1^3\mathrm{H} \). Isobars have the same \( A \) but different \( Z \), so they are different elements, such as \( {}_6^{14}\mathrm{C} \) and \( {}_7^{14}\mathrm{N} \). Isotones share the same neutron number. Scattering experiments show that nuclear volume is proportional to the number of nucleons, so the radius grows only as the cube root of the mass number: \( R=R_0A^{1/3} \) with \( R_0\approx1.2 \) fm. Because mass and volume are both proportional to \( A \), nuclear density is essentially the same for every nucleus, about \( 2.3\times10^{17} \) kg per cubic metre, far beyond any ordinary matter. Heavier nuclei are bigger, not denser, and the radius ratio of two nuclei depends only on the cube root of their mass-number ratio.
topics.worked_example:
Find the radius of \( {}_{13}^{27}\mathrm{Al} \) and compare its density with \( {}_{84}^{216}\mathrm{Po} \) (take \( R_0=1.2 \) fm).

\( R=1.2\times27^{1/3}=1.2\times3=3.6 \) fm.

Radius ratio Po to Al \( =\left(\frac{216}{27}\right)^{1/3}=2 \), but mass and volume both scale with \( A \), so the densities are equal: \( 1:1 \).
common_mistakes: Swapping the definitions: isotopes share \( Z \), isobars share \( A \)
Using \( R\propto A \) instead of \( R\propto A^{1/3} \)
Claiming heavier nuclei are denser; nuclear density is independent of \( A \)
Reporting \( Z \) or \( A \) when asked for the neutron number \( A-Z \)

topics.name: Mass-Energy Equivalence, Mass Defect, and Binding Energy
topics.summary: A nucleus always weighs less than its separate protons and neutrons. The difference is the mass defect, \( \Delta m=[Zm_p+(A-Z)m_n]-M \), taken as constituents minus nucleus so that it is always positive. By Einstein's relation the missing mass appears as the binding energy \( E_b=\Delta mc^2 \): the energy released when free nucleons come together, and equally the energy that must be supplied to pull the nucleus completely apart. The handy conversion is \( 1\text{ u}=931.5\ \text{MeV}/c^2 \). In practice we use atomic masses, replacing each proton with a hydrogen atom; the electrons then appear equally on both sides and cancel exactly. A larger nucleus naturally has a larger total binding energy simply because it has more nucleons, so the total is not a fair measure of stability. To compare nuclei of different sizes, divide by the mass number and use the binding energy per nucleon, \( E_b/A \). The higher this value, the more tightly each nucleon is held and the more stable the nucleus.
common_mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order and getting a negative \( \Delta m \)
Comparing total \( E_b \) of different-sized nuclei to judge stability
Forgetting to convert \( \Delta m \) from u to MeV
Dividing by \( Z \) instead of \( A \) for binding energy per nucleon

topics.name: Nuclear Force and the Binding Energy per Nucleon Curve
topics.summary: The nuclear force holds protons and neutrons together. It is the strongest known force at about 1 fm but has a very short range, vanishing beyond a few femtometres, and becomes strongly repulsive below about 0.8 fm. It is charge-independent, acting almost equally between any pair of nucleons. Because each nucleon attracts only its nearest neighbours, the force saturates. A plot of \( E_b/A \) against \( A \) captures its effects. The curve rises steeply for light nuclei, where many nucleons sit at the surface with few neighbours, with a notable spike at \( {}_2^4\mathrm{He} \). It peaks near \( A\approx56 \) to \( 62 \), the iron-nickel region, at about 8.7 to 8.8 MeV per nucleon. Beyond the peak it falls slowly, because long-range Coulomb repulsion among protons keeps growing while the attraction saturates. This shape explains nuclear energy: heavy nuclei release energy by fission and light nuclei by fusion, because in both cases the products end up with a higher \( E_b/A \), closer to the peak.
topics.worked_example:
A nucleus with \( A=240 \) (\( E_b/A=7.6 \) MeV) splits into two nuclei of \( A=120 \) (\( E_b/A=8.5 \) MeV).

Before: \( 240\times7.6=1824 \) MeV. After: \( 240\times8.5=2040 \) MeV.

Energy released \( =216 \) MeV.
common_mistakes: Thinking the curve rises steadily with \( A \); it peaks near \( A\approx56 \)
Reversing which process suits light and heavy nuclei
Claiming energy is released when products have lower \( E_b/A \)
Treating the nuclear force as long-range or charge-dependent

topics.name: Radioactivity: The Law of Radioactive Decay, Half-Life, and Mean Life
topics.summary: Radioactive decay is random for each nucleus, but a large sample behaves predictably: the decay rate is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei, so \( \frac{dN}{dt}=-\lambda N \), where \( \lambda \) is the decay constant. Integrating gives the exponential law \( N=N_0e^{-\lambda t} \). The half-life \( T_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{\lambda}=\frac{0.693}{\lambda} \) is the time for half the nuclei to decay. After \( n \) half-lives exactly \( \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \) remains, so the sample never reaches zero in any finite time, and each half-life removes half of what is left rather than a fixed amount. The mean life \( \tau=\frac{1}{\lambda} \) is the average lifetime of a nucleus. Since \( T_{1/2}=0.693\tau \), the mean life is always longer than the half-life. Activity \( \mathcal{A}=\lambda N \) counts decays per second, measured in becquerel, where 1 Bq is one decay per second, or in curie, where 1 Ci equals \( 3.7\times10^{10} \) Bq. Activity also halves every half-life, so a sample whose activity drops from 1600 Bq to 100 Bq has passed through four half-lives, because each half-life halves both the number of nuclei and the activity.
topics.worked_example:
A nuclide has \( \tau=10 \) days. How long until \( \frac{1}{8} \) remains?

\( T_{1/2}=0.693\times10=6.93 \) days.

\( \frac{1}{8}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 \), so \( t=3\times6.93=20.79 \) days.
common_mistakes: Treating decay as linear, so the sample empties after two half-lives
Claiming mean life is shorter than or equal to half-life
Confusing activity \( \mathcal{A} \) with the number of nuclei \( N \)
Mixing up becquerel and curie

topics.name: Alpha, Beta, and Gamma Decay; Nuclear Fission and Fusion
topics.summary: Unstable nuclei decay in three main ways. In alpha decay the nucleus emits \( {}_2^4\mathrm{He} \), so \( A \) falls by 4 and \( Z \) by 2. In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, so \( A \) is unchanged and \( Z \) rises by 1; in beta-plus decay a proton becomes a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino, so \( Z \) falls by 1. Because the electron and antineutrino share the released energy, beta electrons show a continuous energy spectrum. Gamma decay is photon emission by an excited nucleus and changes neither \( A \) nor \( Z \). The energy released in any process equals the mass lost times \( c^2 \). In fission, a heavy nucleus such as \( {}_{92}^{235}\mathrm{U} \) absorbs a neutron and splits into two medium fragments plus neutrons, releasing about 200 MeV. In fusion, light nuclei such as deuterium and tritium combine, releasing about 17.6 MeV, which is far more energy per unit mass. Fusion needs temperatures near \( 10^{7} \) K to overcome Coulomb repulsion.
topics.worked_example:
How many alpha and beta-minus decays take \( {}_{92}^{238}\mathrm{U} \) to \( {}_{82}^{206}\mathrm{Pb} \)?

Alpha decays: \( \frac{238-206}{4}=8 \), lowering \( Z \) to \( 92-16=76 \).

Beta-minus decays: \( 82-76=6 \).
common_mistakes: Lowering \( Z \) in beta-minus decay
Changing \( A \) in beta or gamma decay
Swapping the changes in \( A \) and \( Z \) in alpha decay
Subtracting reactant and product masses in the wrong order

questions.question: A sample contains \( 10^{20} \) nuclei of an alpha emitter. How many alpha particles have been emitted after two half-lives?
questions.explanation:
Each decay emits one alpha particle.

Decayed \( =\left(1-\frac{1}{4}\right)\times10^{20}=7.5\times10^{19} \).
questions.hint: One alpha per decay.

questions.question: A sample starts with \( 10^{20} \) nuclei of an alpha emitter, each decay releasing 5 MeV. Taking 1 MeV \( =1.6\times10^{-13} \) J, the energy released in one half-life is
questions.explanation:
Decays in one half-life \( =5\times10^{19} \); energy \( =5\times10^{19}\times5=2.5\times10^{20} \) MeV.

\( 2.5\times10^{20}\times1.6\times10^{-13}=4\times10^{7} \) J.
questions.hint: Only half the nuclei decay in one half-life.

questions.question: A pure sample of a beta-minus emitter decays into a stable daughter. After three half-lives, the ratio of daughter nuclei to parent nuclei is
questions.explanation:
Parent left \( =\frac{1}{8} \); daughters formed \( =\frac{7}{8} \), one per beta decay.

Ratio \( =\frac{7/8}{1/8}=7:1 \).
questions.hint: Each decay creates one daughter.

Gives parent to original, not daughter to parent

questions.question: \( {}_{27}^{60}\mathrm{Co} \) (\( T_{1/2}\approx5.3 \) years) beta-minus decays to an excited \( {}_{28}^{60}\mathrm{Ni}^{*} \), which then emits gamma rays. After 10.6 years, the fraction of the original cobalt remaining and the final ground-state nucleus are
questions.explanation:
\( \frac{10.6}{5.3}=2 \) half-lives, so \( \frac{1}{4} \) remains.

Beta-minus raises \( Z \) to 28 at \( A=60 \); gamma emission leaves \( A \) and \( Z \) unchanged, giving \( {}_{28}^{60}\mathrm{Ni} \).

questions.explanation:
1 Ci \( =3.7\times10^{10} \) decays per second, each emitting one electron.

Per minute: \( 3.7\times10^{10}\times60=2.22\times10^{12} \).

questions.question: 16 mg of \( {}_{86}^{222}\mathrm{Rn} \), an alpha emitter with \( T_{1/2}=3.8 \) days, is sealed in a tube. After 15.2 days, the mass of radon left and the fraction of the original nuclei that have emitted an alpha particle are
questions.explanation:
\( \frac{15.2}{3.8}=4 \) half-lives: \( 16\times\frac{1}{16}=1 \) mg left.

Fraction decayed \( =1-\frac{1}{16}=\frac{15}{16} \), each emitting one alpha particle.
